newsitem.title: USA: CISCO sees per-seat bandwidth doubling.
newsitem.headline: CISCO sees per-seat bandwidth doubling.

text.p: Cisco Systems' top technology executive said congestion on the Internet can be alleviated and the network systems company expects bandwidth per desktop to keep doubling on an annual basis.
"On an annual basis we see the per-desktop bandwidth doubling," said Edward R. Kozel, Cisco chief technology officer and senior vice president, business development.

Addressing Technologic Partners' Internet Outlook conference here, Kozel said that as part of a "wired" future, "extending the infrastructure to fundamentally all parts of our lives has happened, and will continue to happen."
"There is congestion in the Internet but it is we believe easily alleviated," he added in a keynote address, saying he was not aware of any fundamental problems with the Internet.

"We don't see any problems with the Internet architecture other than the problems we know about," he said, adding that known shortcomings in areas such as performance, bandwidth and security would all involve evolutionary changes.

Kozel said certain requirements could increase Internet demand, such as an emerging market for incorporating voice on local area networks, or LANs, to enable the eventual spread of LAN-based telephone switches.
"If they succeed, this will once again double the per- capita consumption of bandwidth," he said, noting that a switched ethernet device would have adequate bandwidth.

The executive noted there are 650,000 companies with 20 to 99 employees expected in the year 2000, with each additional percentage of penetration adding 6,500 companies, a further distribution challenge over the next four years.
Kozel said a convergence of technology in routing and switching would allow the technology of routing to become available with the economics of switching technologies.
He said the market for Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) technology to the desktop was "moribund" in the United States, but would continue to be entrenched in certain world regions.

He said improved firewall technology, used to shield private networks from the public Internet, and the advent of low-cost, high volume, application-specific Internet appliances would also drive Internet use.

Kozel displayed an illustration of what he said would be a small, cheap, simple and easy-to-use 10baseT connection device he said could serve the mass market and function as a full- fledged, personal web-server.

A Web browser could be used to provide a family Internet answering machine, for example, with a choice of leaving voicemail, electronic mail, facsimile, video, periodicals or some combination using existing technologies, he said.

"We are strategically engaged in accelerating this market," he said of the home networking market, which is expected to grow rapidly from nearly nonexistent today to nearly 10 million subscribers in the next five to seven years.

This market would encourage sales of PCs and networking devices for homes, as well as requiring security and address administration for people wanting access to corporate networks and the public Internet.
